episode_title: Justin Brown: I Do Not Have Followers, I Have My People
question: What is the power of consistency in building an online presence and achieving long-term success?
transcript_excerpt: Consistency is the biggest thing you can leverage across all parts of life, whether in your job, social media, or pursuing personal goals. You can win the biggest battle with just consistency—like football and basketball players who work out every day will eventually see positive results. Even without being the most talented or handsome, consistency combined with doing what you love creates momentum and growth that talent alone cannot achieve.

episode_title: Justin Brown: I Do Not Have Followers, I Have My People
question: Why should food content creators focus on video rather than static photography for restaurant reviews?
transcript_excerpt: A picture could trick you, but a video shows you a million words worth of information. When you bite something on video, you can tell if it's tender, see the texture breaking, and observe the genuine reaction—like when someone's eyes close and it takes them back to a memory. That smile and warm feeling on someone's face tells you they really enjoy something, which a picture alone cannot convey.

episode_title: Justin Brown: I Do Not Have Followers, I Have My People
question: What equipment and tools are required to start creating quality food content on a budget?
transcript_excerpt: You don't need expensive equipment—just phones are enough. Get whatever the newest Samsung or iPhone is on the market and the camera will be good enough. Justin uses only smartphones for filming and the free version of CapCut for editing; he invested in a three-thousand-dollar Blackmagic Pocket camera but never used it because phones are simpler and more practical for his workflow.

episode_title: Justin Brown: I Do Not Have Followers, I Have My People
question: How should food reviewers approach writing restaurant reviews compared to creating video content?
transcript_excerpt: When writing, you have to say what the seasoning is and make someone want to go—you cannot just say 'good.' In video, you can simply show whether the food is good, but written articles require more detail to entice readers. You also must be honest about whether the food is worth the money, as that influences whether people will visit the restaurant.

episode_title: Justin Brown: I Do Not Have Followers, I Have My People
question: What philosophy should guide content creators when responding to audience criticism or requests?
transcript_excerpt: If someone asks for directions and you give them correct ones, why would they want you to give them wrong directions too? If people want you to be negative about restaurants you like, that's asking you to be dishonest. By only posting what you like and not what you dislike, you stay true to yourself while still being honest—it's just choosing positivity over negativity.

episode_title: Justin Brown: I Do Not Have Followers, I Have My People
question: Why does service quality and ambiance directly impact how food tastes to a diner?
transcript_excerpt: If your waiter or waitress disrespects you, you won't like the food because you're out of the mood—your taste buds work with you and they have never crossed you. Each person in the restaurant, from the waiter to the chef, plays a major role in the overall food experience, not just the chef alone.

episode_title: Justin Brown: I Do Not Have Followers, I Have My People
question: What is the difference between having followers and building an authentic community?
transcript_excerpt: People have fans, people have followers—I have neither. I have my people. When people meet me and say they're a big fan, I tell them no, you're my people. That's the distinction: followers are transactional, but my people are connected through genuine shared values and authenticity.

episode_title: Justin Brown: I Do Not Have Followers, I Have My People
question: When should a food reviewer give a restaurant a second chance after a poor first experience?
transcript_excerpt: Give everybody two tries because you can have a bad day—everyone does. A different chef or a different waiter or waitress might be there on another day, and each one of these people plays a major role in the food experience. Service quality can completely change your perception of the same restaurant.
